prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable timekeeping at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a clear conceptual idea that was then driven to its limit by experiment. Katori's magic-wavelength trick lets atoms be held in a standing wave of light without shifting the clock transition, so thousands of atoms are interrogated at once with very long coherence. Ye's group took the strontium clock to the 1e-18 regime and showed many-body effects and a direct link to the frequency comb. The result is that one can see the gravitational redshift across a millimetre and test the constancy of fundamental constants. It is exactly the close agreement between a clean theoretical picture and precision measurement that I value, and it was supported by every one of the seven members who ranked it, with four placing it in their top three. Several independent laboratories (Paris, NIST, RIKEN, JILA and others) have reproduced and surpassed the early numbers, and international clock comparisons agree, so the result is robust rather than resting on one measurement. The discovery is mature but the field is still improving, and the discussion of a redefinition of the second makes recognition timely. A two-person single-achievement prize is clean and avoids the allocation problems that trouble most other shortlisted entries.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier prizes: the 2005 prize (Hall and Hansch) for the frequency comb, the 1997 prize for laser cooling, and the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche) for control of single quantum systems and ion clocks already cover much of the toolbox. A sceptical reader can say that lattice clocks are an exceptionally successful refinement and application of recognised ideas rather than a new discovery about nature, and that the main payoff (geodesy, a redefined second) is technological or prospective. Credit is also not perfectly clean: Lemonde, Le Targat and others in Paris, the Boulder and NIST groups, and the ion-clock community contributed, and I am relying on memory for the detailed priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal. This is also the field closest to my own, so I should be careful not to let familiarity inflate my judgement.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B037 first as an unambiguous, clearly defined invention with extensive demonstration, but flagged that the 2012 prize for ion clocks and quantum control might be seen as already recognising the field.
responses.response: I agree with the case and with the qualification. The 2012 prize was for the ability to prepare and read out individual quantum systems, and the ion-clock work was one application. It did not cover the idea that makes the lattice clock work, namely that a single magic wavelength lets one trap a large ensemble without perturbing the transition, which gives both stability and accuracy. That is a distinct conceptual step. I would still keep the citation narrow and tied to the lattice and magic wavelength, so that the prize does not read as a general prize for optical clocks, where the ion-clock credit would be contested.

responses.point: Pearce ranked B037 third and recognised the lasting precision-measurement impact, but noted that ion-clock and Al+ contributions may be seen as comparably decisive and deferred to atomic physicists on relative merit.
responses.response: I will take up the invitation. The Al+ ion clock and the lattice clock achieve similar accuracy through different physics. The ion clock gets its accuracy from having one well-isolated particle, and its stability is limited by the single-ion signal. The lattice clock gets its stability from interrogating a very large number of atoms, and Ye's many-body regime is a separate scientific result about interactions in a degenerate gas. So they are not the same discovery, and the ion-clock work was largely the subject of the 2012 recognition of Wineland. If the committee thinks the ion-clock credit is too entangled, that is a reason to word the citation carefully, not a reason to prefer the Higgs entry, where the allocation problem is far worse.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B006 first as a clear, concrete discovery of nature, the experimental completion of the electroweak sector that the 2013 prize did not honour, while acknowledging that three names are a compromise among thousands.
responses.response: I agree about the scientific importance, and I ranked it sixth because I defer to you on particle physics, not because I doubt the result. My serious reservation is attribution. Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee led the building of the detectors, but the discovery rests on analyses by many people and on the accelerator. A prize that credits leadership while the citation says discovery is something the committee should be able to defend, and I do not yet see how. If the committee can agree that the citation honours conception and construction of the two detectors, I would be more comfortable, and I would keep B006 as a strong alternative. I would not put it ahead of a prize where the three-name limit does not force us to leave out the decisive contributors.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B008) first as the complementary and equally foundational step to the 2025 prize, and openly noted a possible conflict of interest from his proximity to that community.
responses.response: I respect that disclosure and I take the physics seriously: circuit QED is a clean realisation of strong light-matter coupling and a real discovery. My hesitation is the closeness to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits. Two consecutive prizes for superconducting-circuit quantum devices would, in my view, be hard to explain to the wider community, and the allocation also leaves out Girvin, who co-wrote the original proposal. I would be glad to hear whether you think the field is far enough from the 2025 work that the committee can treat it as separate. For this year I place lattice clocks ahead, but I do not regard B008 as weak.

responses.point: Olsson ranked the topological insulator and quantum anomalous Hall entry (B012) first on the strength of a clean prediction-then-measurement chain and wide independent confirmation, while noting that the theory credit may not be fairly limited to the supplied names.
responses.response: I agree that the topological insulator story is an outstanding example of theory confirmed by experiment, and I ranked B042 fifth with the caveat that condensed matter is not my specialty. What troubles me is exactly the point you raise: whether the credit between Kane, Mele, Bernevig, Hughes, Fu, Moore, Molenkamp, Xue and Hasan can be settled by one three-name entry. B012 and B042 give different answers to that, and the fact that two of our colleagues disagree about how to frame the discovery suggests the allocation is not mature, even though the physics certainly is. I am therefore keeping B042 as an alternative, rather than the preferred choice.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a distinct achievement beyond the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for ion control, or as a refinement of them.
How broadly the citation should be drawn: lattice clocks with the magic wavelength only, or optical clocks in general, which would bring in ion-clock and other credit.
The detailed priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal and of the Paris, Boulder and Tokyo demonstrations, which I am recalling from memory.
Whether the topological-insulator entries (B012 versus B042) can be given a defensible three-name credit, since that determines whether I would move them above the clocks.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with B037 is apparent from my profile: I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. I am, however, a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have worked with the Lund and Keller attosecond groups, and I work in the same broad atomic, molecular and optical community as the clock groups, so I should say so openly. None of those connections involves a shortlisted candidate.
